speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The reports also mentioned that he had been facing financial stress at home and that his actions may be a form of coping.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This incident does not mean that every act of mischief stems from mental illness.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But it does bring into sharp focus that mental health challenges are faced by some of our youths, challenges that often remain unseen until they manifest in troubling ways.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They worry about whether treatment will work, fear social stigma or have privacy concerns.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Unfortunately, there is no vaccine for mental illness.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: So, how do we help our children build psychological immunity?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: How do we booster them against the stressors of life?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: As a parent, I worry whether my own children will be able to cope with challenges that come their way.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: As a Singaporean, I worry for our children, who will constitute our future workforce, caregivers and leaders.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When mental well-being falters, it affects not just the individual, but also relationships, families, workplaces and even the fabric of our community.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If we want a resilient Singapore, we must first nurture resilient Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: First, let me clarify what I mean by resilience.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Resilience is not merely the absence of mental illness.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is the ability to bounce forward from setbacks.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Resilience is not something you build after a crisis; it has to be practised before things go wrong.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Just as muscles need to be flexed to grow stronger, resilience must be trained, early, continuously and deliberately.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Especially in schools, where children form habits and mindsets that last a lifetime.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Investing early ensures that every child has the opportunity to build, practice and strengthen these skills across each stage of their development.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Mental resilience must be lived, not lectured, practiced through repetition, reinforced through experience, until these coping habits become second nature so that when stress inevitably comes, these habits are reflexive, automatic and strong enough to carry them through.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Since 2021, the Ministry of Education (MOE) has strengthened its Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) syllabus to include mental health literacy, emotion regulation, coping strategies, stigma reduction and peer support.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Lessons now incorporate breathing and calming exercises, and these are reinforced through Values-in-Action (VIA) projects and co-curricular activities (CCAs).

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A broader ecosystem of support has also been built around this effort: the Parenting for Wellness Toolbox for parents; the scope of examinations for non-graduating students has been reduced; more than 1,000 teacher-counsellors are being trained; and termly check-in surveys allow teachers to monitor students' social-emotional well-being more systematically.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Beyond MOE, national initiatives continue to play an important role.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The Health Promotion Board's (HPB's) It's OKAY to Reach Out campaign and the National Council of Social Service's Beyond the Label movement help normalise help-seeking.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The Agency for Integrated Care's Youth Community Outreach Team (CREST-Youth) and Youth Integrated Teams extend outreach and assessment to at-risk youths.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But as we scale up these initiatives, two key questions remain: how can we ensure these efforts are truly effective and how do we build a school culture that naturally nurtures mental resilience and not just teaches it?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Mental well-being, like literacy or numeracy, is too important to depend on individual school initiatives alone.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: That is why I propose establishing a School Mental Well-being Charter, a developmental accreditation framework that recognises schools embedding mental resilience into their curriculum, culture and community.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We can draw inspiration from the United Kingdom's (UK's) University Mental Health Charter, which brings together universities committed to making mental health a campus-wide priority.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It encourages institutions to share best practices, supports one another through networks and training, and recognises those that demonstrate excellence in promoting mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A Singapore variant, co-led by MOE, HPB and IMH, could serve a similar purpose: uniting schools and Institutes of Higher Learning that make well-being not just an add-on, but a defining feature of education.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This Charter would signal national commitment to nurturing a generation that is mentally strong, emotionally agile and socially compassionate.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: What might such a Charter look like in practice?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: To make it meaningful, it must go beyond slogans and set out clear dimensions of action, balancing centralised standards with decentralised flexibility.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: MOE can provide national direction, resources and guardrails, while schools retain the autonomy to adapt approaches to their unique contexts and students' needs.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: There are three key dimensions where this partnership can be most impactful.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Resilience, like any skill, must be practised, not preached.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: While the CCE curriculum teaches coping and emotion regulation skills, its impact depends on how schools and teachers bring it to life.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Some schools excel through CCAs, camps or VIA projects, others may struggle, constrained by time and resources.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: To make resilience second nature, it cannot remain ad hoc or incidental.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It must be systematic, scaffolded and sustained, so students repeatedly apply, reflect and internalise what they learn.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At the central level, MOE could define broad developmental milestones for social, emotional learning and guiding principles for experiential education, such as structured reflection after setbacks, opportunities for self-directed projects and feedback that emphasises growth over fear of failure.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At the school level, educators could design their own methods through camps, community service, classroom rituals that help students reframe failure as learning.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Micro interventions, when practised consistently, strengthen emotional regulation and self-efficacy over time.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Partnerships with community programmes, like Sport Cares, could also help.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I recently met youths from Sport Cares' Champion Leadership Programme, who organised a carnival for seniors and persons living with dementia.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They were passionate, kind and full of heart, showing how sports and volunteering together can teach grit, empathy and purpose.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: By tapping on community partners, volunteers and youth networks, schools can enrich experiential learning without overstretching educators, allowing them to focus on guiding rather than carrying the process.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Through the Charter, such practices can be shared, refined and scaled so that no students' exposure to resilience building depends purely on which school they attend, because resilience cannot be downloaded from a PowerPoint slide, it must be lived, rehearsed and reinforced again and again until it becomes part of who our students are.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Currently, data on student well-being is often gathered through one-off surveys or teacher observations.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Without a coherent system, we cannot tell which approaches work best for whom and why.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At the central level, MOE could coordinate research using validated measures of subjective well-being, belonging and resilience.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Not to diagnose, but to understand growth and guide interventions.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At the school level, educators could use this data to refine their programmes, track progress over time and share best practices through MOE's networks of practice.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Beyond timely check-ins, such a framework could track both immediate outcomes, such as knowledge and use of coping strategies, and longer-term effects like sustained resilience and belonging.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Crucially, it would shift our focus from identifying problems like anxiety or stress, to measuring strengths, such as happiness, optimism and resilience.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Importantly, this support should extend across every key transition from primary to secondary school, from Institutes of Technical Education, junior colleges, polytechnics to university and eventually into the workforce.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: These are the stages where stress often peaks, yet structured mental health support can taper off.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This approach ensures we do more than collect data.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We also close capability gaps and recognise schools that lead the way.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The goal is not to rank or penalise, but to help every school understand its progress and areas for growth.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It would also allow MOE to identify exemplary practices that can be scaled nationally, creating a culture of shared accountability and collective uplift, because what we choose to measure signals what we value.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And when we value well-being as much as grades, both can thrive together.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Number three, build a supportive and inclusive culture, even with strong programmes and robust data, resilience cannot flourish without the right culture.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Culture determines why it happens and whether change endures.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At the central level, MOE can set the tone through three pillars: wellness, belonging and success.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Well, at the school level, these values are expressed through stories, rituals and daily interactions.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They must be felt in the corridors, classrooms and conversations of every school.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A wellness culture means normalising care through visible practises and spaces, calm corners, reflection, rooms and time-outs that make it acceptable to pause and recharge.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Policies, too, signal what we value, how schools handle phones and screen time, or whether they explore later start times to improve sleep, sends a message that rest is not an indulgence, but a necessity.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Sleep deprivation is not a badge of diligence.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is a silent threat to mental health.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Encouraging sports and outdoor activities, likewise, reinforces well-being.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Exposure to sunlight, physical activity and teamwork all strengthen mental and emotional health.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We can also strengthen peer support networks through structured training and recognition, integrating peer helpers into the school system through accreditation or scholarships.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When peer support is legitimised, help-seeking becomes normalised.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We must move away from labels, like Strawberry Generation or sheltered children.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Such words stigmatise rather than strengthen, they close doors instead of opening minds.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Students also need to feel that they belong, that they are part of something larger than themselves.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This brings me to the second pillar, a school culture of belonging.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Research shows that a strong sense of school belonging is one of the most powerful predictors of resilience.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When students feel seen, supported and accepted, they are better able to cope with setbacks.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: To nurture belonging, schools can foster kindness as a daily habit, encouraging small acts of care, peer recognition and teacher affirmations.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Experiencing kindness, whether online or offline, reinforces connection.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Small everyday gestures of care build the community spirit that sustains well-being.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Our students also need to understand what it truly means to succeed and to redefine success in ways that give meaning, not pressure.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This leads to the third pillar: a success culture.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Singapore has long prized success defined by grades and material achievement.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But true success should include growth, purpose and contribution.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The next step is to embed this shift in school culture, through stories, symbols and rituals that reflect a fuller picture of excellence.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Schools could highlight diverse pathways in assemblies, tell alumni stories that go beyond grades and celebrate perseverance, creativity and community service as much as academic results.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At the same time, culture change also means addressing the unspoken pressures that erode resilience – the tuition race, excessive comparison and the fear of failure.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Reducing rote learning, valuing soft skills and promoting sustainability-oriented values can help students see success as a meaningful living, not mere performance.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Because true resilience is not only about enduring pressure, it is about having the freedom to pursue purpose without being crushed by expectation.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Here again, the Charter can guide this transformation by setting broad cultural benchmarks for schools to interpret locally: do students feel psychological safety and belonging?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Are conversations about mental health open and stigma-free?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In essence, practice builds skills and habits, measurement builds accountability and learning, and culture builds meaning and motivation.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Together, they form a resilience ecosystem, where each reinforces the other.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Practice without culture becomes tokenism; measurement without practice risks bureaucracy; culture without structure leads to inconsistency.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Rather than ranking schools, it would celebrate those that lead with care, helping others to learn and grow.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Dr Chen, you may want to round up soon.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: By aligning our children's mental well-being with our broader national ambition, we give meaning to the spirit of Forward Singapore – building a nation that is vibrant, fair, thriving, resilient and united.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: She mentioned three broad points in relation to strengthening practice and experiential learning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Building our students' mental resilience is a key priority for MOE, just as learning is for us; and the CCE curriculum is a key enabler.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: CCE is guided by developmental milestones, which indicate the requisite knowledge, habits and skills students will need at pertinent junctures in their respective educational journeys.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: And as our students progress from primary to tertiary levels, they will cumulatively build up their social and emotional capacity, as well as their resilience.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These equip our students with the knowledge and skills to cope with stressors and maintain their mental well-being.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Older students also explore relevant topics such as stigmatisations, unhealthy social comparisons, as well as the awareness of potentially negative impact of digital lifestyles, such as poor sleep and overly sedentary habits.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: CCE also covers cyber wellness topics that can affect the mental health of our students, including excessive screen use, unhealthy or inappropriate media content, cyberbullying, as well as the fear of missing out (FOMO).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Students are taught skills to recognise such risks in the digital space, and identify and discern negative influences, as well as adopt a more balanced use of social media.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Beyond classroom lessons, Mr Speaker, students are encouraged to practise what they have learnt through other student developmental experiences as well, such as the CCAs, sports and games, visual and performing arts, and outdoor education activities, school camps and VIA projects.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Teachers and coaches provide guidance to help students apply relevant knowledge and skills in real world context for better internalisation and reinforcement of the lessons learnt.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: To help schools better facilitate students learning beyond the classroom, MOE provides guidance on how schools can structure their student development experiences to promote social and emotional learning, including the reinforcement of resilient mindset and skills.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Further to this, the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) then build on the CCE efforts in the earlier years, and avail a range of mental well-being programmes and activities to their students, including modules and workshops on topics like positive psychology, to teach students how to manage their setbacks better.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Even as MOE HQ provides the broad guidance and baseline curriculum provisions and guidelines, I would like to reassure Dr Chen that there is no lack of initiatives from our schools, or even the students themselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: For example, schools have designed their own programmes to promote the "Growth Mindset" in their students and supported student-led activities, such as the Mental Wellness Day.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Centrally, MOE does provide platforms for schools to share their best practices to others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: This is similar to the charter that the Member has raised, and just last week, in fact, CCE key personnel from all secondary schools gathered to hear about the latest developments in CCE and to discuss their school initiatives with others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: For example, Pasir Ris Secondary shared about their efforts to build students everyday resilience, not only through CCE lessons, but also through peer support networks, through camps and even after-school programmes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Recognising that programmes alone are insufficient, the school leadership also build this emphasis into their staff culture, into the school's strategic plans, as well as in the everyday language of communication in school.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: MOE will continue to tap on the passion, the ideas and the efforts from the ground to complement our efforts as well.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: In our schools and IHLs, educators are at the frontline where students' well-being is concerned.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: They help students feel understood, supported and cared for.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: And through their daily interactions with students, educators are often the first ones to detect an unhappy student and to offer their first words of support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Our educators certainly do not work alone but are part of a larger support system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: The IHLs similarly collaborate with social service agencies to expand their range of outreach programmes and promote holistic well-being as well.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Peers are also integral to every school's ecosystem of support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Peer support leaders have been identified in every school and are trained to provide a listening ear to their friends and encourage help-seeking early.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: All students are also taught about peer support in CCE where they learn to look out for and show care to one another.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: In our IHLs, some also have institution-wide peer supporter programmes while others have dedicated ones housed within their schools or faculties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Dr Chen has reminded us that resilience cannot flourish without the right culture.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Through empowering our educators, building student peer support networks and strengthening the schools' referral system, we seek to foster a stronger supportive culture as highlighted by the Member.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Besides relying on data, MOE also engages relevant experts, professionals and community partners to regularly receive inputs regarding the mental health needs and challenges of our youths.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: I also want to assure the Member that MOE regularly reviews and refreshes our curriculum and strategies to keep up with the students' evolving needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Our CCE and mental resilience building efforts, including the curation of topics and pedagogical approaches, are evidence-informed and age-appropriate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: We also have internal mechanisms to monitor the implementation of our CCE curriculum and programmes, and regularly obtain feedback from stakeholders to ensure that our efforts have the intended and positive desired impact for our students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: IHLs also similarly deploy a range of sensing mechanisms, such as well-being surveys, campus walkabouts and town hall sessions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: All our tracking and review efforts, at MOE and the varying school levels, are part of our culture-building endeavour to strengthen awareness of and commitment to student well-being.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Dr Syed Harun, you might want to round up.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: And finally, the Member's call for a strong culture of resilience-building resonates with us.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: In this, the family plays a critical role, and the best support for our children happens when schools and parents work in close partnership.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: And in this respect, MOE also supports parents with resources, supporting their child's strengths and interests and regulating emotions.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: These are shared through our platforms such as the Parents Gateway and parent support groups.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: In education, we believe that our role is not to remove stressors entirely from the lives of our young nor to rescue them from all of their difficulties.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: This is only possible with the whole of society onboard – parents, community and educators.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Pursuant to Standing Order 2(3)(a), I wish to inform hon Members that the Sitting tomorrow will commence at 10.30 am.
